TeleDirectMD is a physician-owned, MD-only telehealth practice operating in 41 states plus Washington, DC, and no nurse practitioners or physician assistants treat children here. TeleDirectMD limits telehealth eczema care to low- and mid-potency topical steroids, steroid-sparing agents, and bland emollients; we do not prescribe oral or systemic steroids or biologics online, and refer severe or refractory eczema to in-person dermatology. Self-pay visits are $79, and TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances.

telehealthRegulations.sectionTitle: Telehealth Regulations Across Our Licensed States
paragraphs: TeleDirectMD operates only where its physicians hold active licensure, currently 41 states plus Washington, DC. Each state sets its own telemedicine standards, and in every state a parent or legal guardian must consent to a minor's care. TeleDirectMD verifies that the child is physically located in a licensed state at the time of the visit; care is not provided to children outside the licensed footprint.

Some states limit the potency class of topical steroids that may be prescribed for pediatric patients by telehealth without a follow-up visit. State-specific pages cite the controlling state statute. TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances.

paragraphs: Eczema (atopic dermatitis) is a chronic, relapsing, itchy inflammatory skin condition driven by a weakened skin barrier and an overactive immune response. It causes dry, red, scaly, intensely itchy patches, classically in the elbow and knee creases in children.

Eczema is part of the 'atopic march' alongside asthma and allergies and is managed with moisturizers and topical anti-inflammatories. The American Academy of Dermatology atopic dermatitis guidelines (2023 update) and the published pediatric evidence base summarize first-line care: daily emollients plus topical anti-inflammatory therapy during flares.

TeleDirectMD focuses on mild-to-moderate eczema in children ages 5 to 17 that can be evaluated by video, with a parent present, and refers severe, widespread, or infected eczema to in-person dermatology.

causesAndRiskFactors.sectionTitle: Causes and Risk Factors in Children
causesAndRiskFactors.intro: Pediatric eczema in children ages 5 to 17 has several recognized causes and contributors:

items.label: Genetic skin-barrier dysfunction:
items.text: including filaggrin gene variants that weaken the skin barrier.

items.label: Personal or family history of atopy:
items.text: a history of eczema, asthma, or hay fever increases risk.

items.label: Triggers:
items.text: dry air, heat and sweat, harsh soaps, wool, and stress can provoke flares.

items.label: Allergens and irritants:
items.text: contact with allergens and irritants can flare the skin.

items.label: Skin infection:
items.text: infection, often with Staphylococcus aureus, can worsen flares.

causesAndRiskFactors.closing: Not every itchy rash is eczema. Contact dermatitis, psoriasis, tinea (ringworm), scabies, and infected eczema can all mimic atopic dermatitis. TeleDirectMD uses history and video exam to distinguish them and directs atypical or severe presentations to in-person evaluation.

compareCards.title: Eczema vs Contact Dermatitis
compareCards.text: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic, itchy, flexural rash in a child with an atopic history (eczema, asthma, or hay fever). Contact dermatitis instead matches a specific exposure pattern, such as a nickel reaction under a snap or jewelry, or a linear rash from a plant. The distribution and history help a physician tell them apart by video.

compareCards.title: Eczema vs Psoriasis, Tinea, and Scabies
compareCards.text: Psoriasis produces well-defined plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces and scalp, unlike eczema's flexural, itchy patches. Tinea (ringworm) shows a ring-shaped scaly border with central clearing and is fungal. Scabies causes intense night itch with burrows in the web spaces and is contagious. Infected eczema shows weeping, crusting, or pustules and may need antibiotics.

differentialDiagnosis.closing: If the eczema is severe, widespread, infected, or there are signs of eczema herpeticum, TeleDirectMD will direct you to in-person or emergency care.

treatmentOptions.intro: The foundation of eczema care is daily moisturizing plus a topical anti-inflammatory during flares. TeleDirectMD physicians match steroid potency to the body site (low-potency for face and folds, mid-potency for body) and may use steroid-sparing agents for sensitive areas, with clear flare and maintenance instructions.

sections.title: Daily emollient routine
sections.text: Apply a thick, fragrance-free cream or ointment at least twice daily, especially after bathing. Take short lukewarm baths, pat dry, and seal in moisture within three minutes. This emollient foundation is the most important part of eczema control for children ages 5 to 17.

sections.title: Topical anti-inflammatories for flares
sections.text: Low-potency hydrocortisone is used on the face and skin folds, with mid-potency triamcinolone, fluocinolone, or mometasone for the body. Topical steroids are applied only to active patches for the directed duration. Steroid-sparing agents such as tacrolimus or crisaborole are options for sensitive areas.

sections.title: Trigger reduction
sections.text: Identify and reduce triggers such as dry air, heat and sweat, harsh soaps, wool, and stress. Use gentle, fragrance-free cleansers, keep nails short, and consider cotton gloves at night to limit scratching damage. Good maintenance care lengthens the time between flares.

sections.title: When to escalate
sections.text: Return for in-person care if the skin becomes weepy, crusted, or infected, if flares do not respond, or if there are signs of eczema herpeticum. Severe or widespread eczema needing systemic therapy or biologics is managed by in-person dermatology.

homeCare.sectionTitle: Home Care, Recovery Timeline, Prevention, and Follow-up

whatToDoNow.title: Timeline and What to Do Now
items: Moisturize at least twice daily with a thick fragrance-free cream or ointment, especially after bathing.
Take short lukewarm baths and pat dry, then seal with moisturizer within 3 minutes.
Apply the prescribed topical steroid only to active patches for the directed duration.
Use gentle fragrance-free cleansers and avoid wool and known irritants.

whatToWatch.title: What to Watch For During Treatment
items: If skin becomes weepy, crusted, or develops honey-colored crusts or pustules, watch for secondary infection.
If painful clustered blisters with fever develop, seek emergency care for possible eczema herpeticum.
If flares do not respond to treatment, follow up by video or seek in-person care.
Keep nails short and consider cotton gloves at night to reduce scratching damage.

followUp.title: Prevention and Follow-up
items: Continue daily moisturizing even when the skin looks clear to lengthen the time between flares.
Identify and reduce triggers such as dry air, heat, harsh soaps, and wool.
Use the prescribed topical anti-inflammatory only on active patches during flares.
Return for in-person care if skin becomes infected or if flares do not respond.
Follow up by video if the eczema is not improving as expected.

items.question: Can TeleDirectMD treat my child's eczema online?
items.answer: Yes, for mild-to-moderate cases. TeleDirectMD treats eczema (atopic dermatitis, ICD-10 L20.9) by video for children ages 5 to 17 with a parent present. An MD assesses the rash and prescribes moisturizer routines plus low- to mid-potency topical steroids or steroid-sparing agents. The self-pay visit is $79, available in 41 states plus Washington, DC. Severe or infected eczema is referred to in-person dermatology.

items.question: What eczema medications can TeleDirectMD prescribe for a child?
items.answer: For children ages 5 to 17, TeleDirectMD physicians prescribe low-potency hydrocortisone (all ages) for the face and skin folds, mid-potency triamcinolone or fluocinolone for the body, mometasone (ages 2+), and steroid-sparing options such as tacrolimus (ages 2+) or crisaborole (ages 3 months+). TeleDirectMD does not prescribe oral or systemic steroids or biologics online and refers severe eczema to dermatology.

items.question: How is eczema treated besides medication?
items.answer: The foundation of eczema care is daily moisturizing. TeleDirectMD counsels parents of children ages 5 to 17 to apply a thick fragrance-free cream or ointment at least twice daily, take short lukewarm baths and seal in moisture within three minutes, use gentle cleansers, and avoid wool and known irritants. Topical anti-inflammatories are added only on active patches during flares.

items.question: When does my child's eczema need in-person or specialist care?
items.answer: See in-person dermatology, not TeleDirectMD, if a child ages 5 to 17 has severe or widespread eczema needing systemic therapy or biologics, eczema that is weeping, crusted, or pustular (suggesting infection), or painful clustered blisters with fever, which can indicate eczema herpeticum, a medical emergency. TeleDirectMD treats mild-to-moderate eczema online with topical therapy and emollients.

items.question: Will TeleDirectMD prescribe a strong steroid for my child's eczema?
items.answer: No. TeleDirectMD limits telehealth eczema care for children ages 5 to 17 to low- and mid-potency topical steroids, steroid-sparing agents, and emollients, matching potency to the body site (low-potency for face and folds). High-potency steroids, oral or systemic steroids, and biologics are not prescribed online; children needing them are referred to in-person dermatology for monitoring.

items.question: Does a parent need to be present for an eczema visit?
items.answer: Yes. A parent or legal guardian must be present for the entire visit and provide consent for any child ages 5 to 17 seen by TeleDirectMD for eczema. The guardian's identity is verified, and the child must be physically located in one of the 41 states plus Washington, DC where TeleDirectMD is licensed at the time of the video visit.

items.question: Is eczema curable, or just managed?
items.answer: Eczema (atopic dermatitis) is a chronic, relapsing condition that is managed rather than cured, and many children improve as they grow older. TeleDirectMD helps families of children ages 5 to 17 control flares with a daily moisturizing routine and topical anti-inflammatories, and reduce triggers such as dry air, heat, harsh soaps, and wool. Good maintenance care lengthens the time between flares.

items.question: How much does an online pediatric eczema visit cost?
items.answer: An online pediatric eczema visit at TeleDirectMD costs $79 self-pay, no insurance required, for children ages 5 to 17. TeleDirectMD is in-network with Aetna, select Blue Cross Blue Shield plans, and UnitedHealthcare where applicable, but is not in-network with any Medicaid, Managed Medicaid, CHIP, or Medicare-Medicaid plan in any state.

items.question: Can eczema get infected, and how is that handled?
items.answer: Yes. Eczema can become secondarily infected, often with Staphylococcus aureus, showing weeping, honey-colored crusts, or pustules. If a TeleDirectMD physician identifies limited secondary infection in a child ages 5 to 17, treatment may include topical therapy; more extensive infection or suspected eczema herpeticum (painful clustered blisters with fever) is referred for urgent in-person care.

items.question: Does TeleDirectMD treat eczema in children under 5?
items.answer: No. TeleDirectMD treats eczema only for children ages 5 to 17. Although several eczema medications are labeled for younger children, TeleDirectMD's pediatric skin services begin at age 5. Infants and toddlers with eczema should be managed by their pediatrician, who can confirm the diagnosis, guide moisturizing routines, and select age-appropriate topical therapy in person.

paragraphs: This page is informational and is not a substitute for in-person medical care. TeleDirectMD treats children ages 5 to 17 for eczema; we do not treat children under age 5 for any condition (ages 0 to 4 are excluded). A parent or legal guardian must be present for the entire visit and provide consent, and the child must be physically located in a licensed state (41 states plus Washington, DC) at the time of the visit.

TeleDirectMD does not prescribe controlled substances or isotretinoin, does not diagnose or treat mental health conditions or ADHD, does not make new asthma diagnoses, and does not prescribe oral or systemic corticosteroids or biologics by telehealth. Any infant under 3 months with fever requires emergency care. TeleDirectMD is not in-network with any Medicaid, Managed Medicaid, CHIP, or Medicare-Medicaid plan in any state.
